status: drafted via direct read of the real Geneva Bible (1560) extracted verse text, cross-referenced against the existing KJV Galatians.json for structural precedent only
notes: Galatians in the Geneva translation tells exactly the same story, in the same 6-chapter structure, as the KJV version of this book — Paul's autobiographical defense of his apostleship (his conversion, two visits to Jerusalem, and the public confrontation with Peter at Antioch) followed by sustained doctrinal argument against a Judaizing faction demanding circumcision of Gentile converts. There is no Ezra-style structural/canon divergence here; every KJV pericope (justification by faith, the law's temporary role and believers' adoption as sons, the Hagar/Sarah allegory, the fruit of the Spirit versus works of the flesh, and closing burden-bearing instructions) is present in the same order with the same argument. The real differences found by reading the actual Geneva text are wording-level, not content-level, and are worth flagging rather than silently normalizing to KJV phrasing: (1) Galatians 2:3 calls Titus "a Grecian" where KJV has "a Greek," and the same word choice repeats at 3:28 ("There is neither Iewe nor Grecian" vs. KJV's "neither Jew nor Greek"); (2) the Hagar/Sarah allegory (4:22-26) spells her name "Agar," an archaic transliteration of the same figure, not a different person or a naming collision; (3) the works-of-the-flesh catalogue at 5:19-21 ends "...Enuie, murthers, drunkennesse, gluttonie, and such like" — Geneva's "gluttonie" stands where the KJV list instead has "revellings" as its final named vice before "and such like," a genuine translation-choice difference in this specific list, not an invented addition to the text. Tier structure mirrors the KJV precedent for this book: two person-tiers carry the letter's only embodied narrative action (Paul throughout; Peter specifically for the Antioch incident, 2:11-14, where he acts, is confronted, and visibly changes behavior under social pressure), while the doctrinal core is captured as four law/theme tiers, all deliveredBy Paul since he is the letter's sole author and voice — there is no separate transmitter relaying content from someone else, unlike the Pentateuch's Moses-delivers-God's-law pattern. Barnabas and Titus are submanagers under Paul (his companions to the Jerusalem council, 2:1-10, with Titus serving as the chapter's live test case for Gentile freedom from circumcision); James "the Lord's brother" and John are submanagers under Peter, both named only in the "pillars" passage (2:9), with James named again as the source of the men whose arrival at Antioch prompted Peter's withdrawal (2:12). The unnamed Judaizers/false brethren (1:6-7; 2:4; 5:10,12; 6:12-13) are collapsed into one collective submanager under Paul, since the Geneva text — like the KJV — never individuates members of this group. Peter/Cephas naming: within this Geneva text specifically, "Peter" is used at 1:18, 2:7, 2:8, 2:11, and 2:14, while "Cephas" appears only once, at 2:9 — the identical distribution found in the KJV text of this same book, so no translation-specific naming divergence exists here despite the archaic spelling elsewhere. James "the Lord's brother" (1:19) is distinct from the apostles James son of Zebedee and James son of Alphaeus, neither of whom is otherwise distinguished by that title in this letter; "Iohn" (2:9) is presumed to be the apostle son of Zebedee though the text gives no further identifying detail, and is not John the Baptist, who does not appear in this letter.

scribeTiers.scribeName: The Markes of the Lord Iesus
The Iust Shall Liue by Faith

characters.name: Paul (Pavl)
characters.scribeTier: The Markes of the Lord Iesus

genealogy.mother: unnamed — Galatians 1:15 ("which had separated me from my mothers wombe")

verses.note: Opens: "Pavl an Apostle (not of men, neither by man, but by Iesus Christ, and God the Father which hath raised him from the dead)."
"The Gospel which was preached of me, was not after man. For neither receiued I it of man, neither was I taught it, but by the reuelation of Iesus Christ."
Recounts persecuting and wasting the Church of God "extremely" in his former life in the Jewish religion, exceeding his peers, "much more zealous of the traditions of my fathers."

God, having separated him from his mother's womb and called him by grace, revealed His Son in him to preach among the Gentiles; he did not confer with flesh and blood but went into Arabia, then returned to Damascus.
After three years came to Jerusalem "to visite Peter, and abode with him fifteene dayes," seeing no other apostle save James the Lord's brother.
Fourteen years later went up to Jerusalem again with Barnabas, taking Titus also, by revelation, and privately declared the Gospel he preaches among the Gentiles.
"When Peter was come to Antiochia, I withstood him to his face: for he was to be condemned." Publicly rebukes Peter before all for compelling Gentiles to live as Jews.
"I am crucified with Christ, but I liue, yet not I any more, but Christ liueth in me" — states the core of his justification-by-faith theology in personal terms.
Recalls that "through infirmitie of the flesh, I preached ye Gospel vnto you at the first," and that the Galatians received him "as an Angel of God, yea, as Christ Iesus."
"My litle children, of whome I trauaile in birth againe, vntill Christ be formed in you" — a direct, anguished personal appeal.
"Ye see how large a letter I haue written vnto you with mine owne hand" — emphasizes the letter's personal authorship.
"I beare in my body the markes of the Lord Iesus" — closes asserting his authority through physical suffering endured for Christ.

funFacts: The Geneva text's opening self-identification, "Pavl an Apostle," preserves the period's u/v typographic convention ("Pavl" for "Paul") throughout this 1560 printing.

Galatians 1-2 is one of Paul's most detailed autobiographical passages in any of his letters, given specifically to prove his gospel came directly from Christ rather than secondhand from the Jerusalem apostles.

characters.name: Peter (Cephas)

verses.note: Paul goes to Jerusalem specifically "to visite Peter," abiding with him fifteen days.

Recognized as a "pillar" alongside James and John; the Gospel over the circumcision was committed to Peter as it was to Paul over the uncircumcision; perceiving the grace given to Paul, gives Paul and Barnabas "the right hands of fellowship."
"Peter was come to Antiochia" and Paul withstood him to his face, "for he was to be condemned."

Ate with the Gentiles until certain men came from James, "then he withdrew and separated himselfe, fearing them which were of the Circumcision"; the other Jews, and even Barnabas, followed his hypocrisy.
Publicly rebuked by Paul: "If thou being a Iewe, liuest as the Gentiles, and not like the Iewes, why constrainest thou the Gentiles to doe like the Iewes?"

funFacts: This Geneva text names him "Peter" at 1:18, 2:7, 2:8, 2:11, and 2:14, and "Cephas" only once, at 2:9 — the identical naming distribution found in this project's KJV text of the same letter, so no translation-specific naming divergence exists for this figure despite the archaic spelling elsewhere in this printing.

characters.name: Barnabas
characters.scribeTier: The Markes of the Lord Iesus

verses.note: Accompanies Paul on his second visit to Jerusalem.
Given the right hands of fellowship alongside Paul by James, Cephas, and John.
"Barnabas was led away with them by that their hypocrisie" — withdraws from eating with Gentiles at Antioch along with Peter and the other Jews, a real, textually-stated lapse.

characters.name: Titus
characters.scribeTier: The Markes of the Lord Iesus

verses.note: Taken by Paul to Jerusalem alongside Barnabas.

"Neither yet Titus which was with me, though he were a Grecian, was compelled to be circumcised" — this Geneva text's own wording, "a Grecian" (where the KJV reads "a Greek"), serves as the letter's live test case for Gentile freedom from the law.

funFacts: The Geneva translation's word choice "Grecian" for Titus at 2:3 recurs at 3:28's "neither Iewe nor Grecian" — a consistent translation preference in this printing, not a one-off.

characters.name: Iames, the Lords Brother
characters.perkNote: NAMING COLLISION: this is James "the Lord's brother" (1:19), a leader of the Jerusalem church — not the apostle James son of Zebedee (brother of John) nor the apostle James son of Alphaeus, neither of whom is otherwise distinguished by that title in this letter. Galatians 2:9 shows him personally extending the right hand of fellowship to Paul and Barnabas as one of the three Jerusalem "pillars," a directly supportive act, even though 2:12 also notes men associated with him prompted Peter's withdrawal at Antioch — loyalty-boost fits the more textually direct relationship to Peter's tier.

verses.note: The only other apostle Paul saw in Jerusalem besides Peter on his first post-conversion visit: "none other of the Apostles sawe I, saue Iames the Lords brother."
Named alongside Cephas and John as one of the Jerusalem "pillars" who gave Paul and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship.
"For before that certaine came from Iames" — the arrival of men associated with James is what prompts Peter to withdraw from eating with the Gentiles at Antioch.

funFacts: Described in the text itself as "the Lords brother" (1:19), a family relationship to Jesus stated directly by Paul.

characters.name: Iohn
characters.perkNote: NAMING COLLISION: named only once, in the list of Jerusalem "pillars" (2:9); presumed to be the apostle John son of Zebedee, though the text gives no further identifying detail — not to be confused with John the Baptist, who does not appear anywhere in this letter.

verses.note: Named alongside James and Cephas as a "pillar" apostle who gave Paul and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship.

characters.name: The Troublers / False Brethren
characters.scribeTier: The Markes of the Lord Iesus
characters.perkNote: Collective entry covering multiple related but textually undifferentiated opposition references (1:6-7; 2:4's "false brethren"; 5:10; 5:12; 6:12-13) — the Geneva text, like the KJV, never names or individually distinguishes members of this group, so per the indexing rule against inventing differentiation, they are recorded as one collective rather than as separate invented individuals.

verses.note: "I marueile that ye are so soone remoued away vnto another Gospel... some which trouble you, and intend to peruert the Gospel of Christ."
"The false brethren which were craftily sent in, and crept in priuily to spie out our libertie, which we haue in Christ Iesus, that they might bring vs into bondage."
"Hee that troubleth you, shall beare his condemnation, whosoeuer he be."
"Would to God they were euen cut off, which doe disquiet you."

"As many as desire to make a faire shewe in the flesh, they constraine you to be circumcised, onely because they would not suffer persecution for the crosse of Christ. For they themselues which are circumcised keepe not the law, but desire to haue you circumcised, that they might reioyce in your flesh."

characters.name: Justification by Faith, Not Workes of the Law
characters.scribeTier: The Iust Shall Liue by Faith
characters.purpose: Refutes the Judaizers' demand that Gentile believers keep the Mosaic law (especially circumcision) to be justified before God; establishes that righteousness comes by faith in Jesus Christ, not by works of the law, following directly from the Antioch confrontation with Peter.

verses.note: "A man is not iustified by the works of the Law, but by ye faith of Iesus Christ... because that by the workes of the Lawe, no flesh shalbe iustified."
"I am crucified with Christ"; "if righteousnes be by the Lawe, then Christ dyed without a cause."
"Receiued ye the Spirit by the workes of the Lawe, or by the hearing of faith preached?"
"As Abraham beleeued God, and it was imputed to him for righteousnes"; "they which be of faith, are blessed with faithfull Abraham."
"As many as are of the workes of the Lawe, are vnder the curse"; "the iust shall liue by faith"; Christ redeemed believers from the curse of the Law, "made a curse for vs."
"The Lawe was our scholemaster to bring vs to Christ, that we might be made righteous by faith."

characters.name: The Lawes Purpose, Sonship, and Libertie in Christ
characters.purpose: Explains the temporary, preparatory role of the Mosaic law relative to God's earlier promise to Abraham, describes believers' adoption as sons and heirs through Christ, and — via the allegory of Agar and the free woman — contrasts bondage under the law with freedom in Christ, urging the Galatians not to return to that bondage by accepting circumcision.

verses.note: The covenant confirmed to Abraham, and the Law which came four hundred and thirty years after, cannot disannul that earlier promise.
"Wherefore then serueth the Law? It was added because of the transgressions, til the seed came."

"Ye are al the sonnes of God by faith, in Christ Iesus... There is neither Iewe nor Grecian: there is neither bonde nor free: there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Iesus" — this Geneva text's own wording, "Grecian," rather than "Greek."

"God sent forth his Sonne made of a woman, and made vnder the Lawe, That hee might redeeme them which were vnder the Law"; God sends forth the Spirit of His Son into believers' hearts, "which crieth, Abba, Father."
Warns against turning again to "impotent and beggerly rudiments" and observing "dayes, and moneths, and times and yeeres."

The allegory of Agar and the free woman: "these mothers are the two testaments, the one which is Agar of mount Sina, which gendreth vnto bondage... Hierusalem, which is aboue, is free: which is the mother of vs all" — this Geneva printing's own spelling, "Agar," an archaic transliteration of the same figure elsewhere rendered "Hagar."
"Put out the seruant and her sonne"; believers are children of the free woman, not the servant.
"Stand fast therefore in the libertie wherewith Christ hath made vs free, and be not intangled againe with the yoke of bondage."
"Ye are abolished from Christ: whosoeuer are iustified by the Law, ye are fallen from grace."
"A litle leauen doeth leauen the whole lumpe" — warns how a small compromise (accepting circumcision) corrupts the whole.

characters.name: The Fruite of the Spirit vs. the Workes of the Flesh
characters.purpose: Contrasts the visible outcomes of living by sinful human nature ("the flesh") with the character produced by the Holy Spirit, instructing believers to walk in the Spirit rather than gratify the flesh — the practical, ethical expression of the freedom just described.

verses.note: "Walke in the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfill the lustes of the flesh. For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary one to another."

Lists the works of the flesh — "adulterie, fornication, vncleannes, wantonnes, Idolatrie, witchcraft, hatred, debate, emulations, wrath, contentions, seditions, heresies, Enuie, murthers, drunkennesse, gluttonie, and such like" — a genuine Geneva-specific wording, ending in "gluttonie" where the KJV list instead ends in "revellings" before "and such like"; warns that "they which doe such things, shall not inherite the kingdome of God."
Lists the fruit of the Spirit — "loue, ioye, peace, long suffering, gentlenes, goodnes, fayth, Meekenesse, temperancie: against such there is no lawe."
"They that are Christes, haue crucified the flesh with the affections and the lustes. If we liue in the Spirit, let vs also walke in the Spirit."

characters.name: Bearing One Anothers Burden; Sowing to the Spirit
characters.purpose: Practical instruction for community life among believers — restoring those suddenly taken in an offence, sharing one another's burdens, supporting teachers, and the principle that what a person sows (to the flesh or to the Spirit) determines what they will reap — closing the letter's ethical instruction just before its final warnings about the circumcision party.

verses.note: If a man "be suddenly taken in any offence," the spiritual are to restore such a one "with the spirit of meekenes."
"Beare ye one anothers burden, and so fulfill the Lawe of Christ."
"For euery man shall beare his owne burden."
"Let him that is taught in the worde, make him that hath taught him, partaker of all his goods."

"Whatsoeuer a man soweth, that shall hee also reape... hee that soweth to his flesh, shall of the flesh reape corruption: but hee that soweth to the spirit, shall of the spirit reape life euerlasting."
"Let vs not therefore be weary of well doing... let vs doe good vnto all men, but specially vnto them, which are of the housholde of faith."

genealogyLists.note: Bulk or deliberately-unresolved references, kept out of the character list above.

churchesOfGalatia.note: The letter's addressees — "the Churches of Galatia," a collective of congregations in the Roman province of Galatia, not individually named or indexed.

churchesOfJudea.note: "I was vnknowen by face vnto the Churches of Iudea, which were in Christ" — congregations who had only heard secondhand of Paul's conversion; mentioned collectively, never as individuals.

themOfTheCircumcision.note: The party in Jerusalem/Antioch whose arrival caused Peter to withdraw from eating with Gentiles — substantially overlaps with the Judaizers/false brethren submanager entry above; the text does not name individuals within this group.
